strengths: First systematic study of 4-bit quantization-aware training for attention: Identifies and rigorously addresses a real, important problem in efficient neural networks that prior work hasn't systematically tackled.

Sound technical solution with minimal added complexity: Proposes a principled QAT approach that recovers model quality without requiring complex outlier mitigation heuristics (unlike SageAttention3), making it more deployable.

Comprehensive experimental validation across domains: Evaluates on diverse models (diffusion 1.3B-14B, LLMs 3B-70B) and benchmarks (VBench, WikiText, MMLU, mathematical reasoning), demonstrating broad applicability.

Clear problem demonstration with significant quality impact: Shows dramatic quality degradation from naive FP4 quantization (VBench 0.833→0.325), establishing necessity of the approach and validating the motivation.

Detailed algorithm specification and reproducibility resources: Algorithms 1-3 are clearly specified; Appendix B provides hyperparameters, training details, and implementation notes supporting reproducibility.
Excellent qualitative visualization: Figures 6-8 provide compelling visual comparisons showing Attn-QAT achieves quality comparable to BF16 baseline, strengthening claims beyond numerical metrics.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core technique (QAT) is well-established; contribution primarily involves careful application to attention with engineering modifications rather than introducing new methodological concepts.

Insufficient mechanistic explanation: While identifying what fails (precision mismatches), the paper provides limited intuition for why attention is disproportionately sensitive to 4-bit quantization compared to other components—the dramatic quality degradation seems out of proportion to the technical issues described.

Incomplete analysis of training overhead: Solution requires maintaining both FP32 and FP4 tensors during training, but memory and computational overhead during training are not quantified or thoroughly discussed.
Narrow scope of insights: Contributions are specific to attention mechanisms rather than broadly applicable across architectures, limiting the generalizability of insights to other model components.

Dense technical presentation: Sections 2.1-2.3 are notation-heavy; the backward pass analysis (Algorithm 3, equations 8-9) would benefit from more intuitive explanation before mathematical details. Notation φ(·) and ψ(·) usage inconsistently clarified.

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons to other recent QAT variants or precision-matching quantization schemes beyond SageAttention3, making it unclear whether vanilla QAT is optimal or if more sophisticated approaches might be better.

Modest practical speedup: 1.5x inference speedup (Figure 5) must be weighed against additional training requirements and dual-precision overhead, raising questions about real-world deployment benefits.

Incomplete evaluation scenarios: LLM experiments use continued training rather than post-training quantization, which doesn't reflect typical deployment where pre-trained weights are quantized without additional fine-tuning budget.
Missing ablation studies: No evaluation of 8-bit attention, other precision formats for fake quantization, or sensitivity analysis of hyperparameter choices.
Code unavailability: Implementation not yet available for verification; future reproducibility depends on timely code release.
